utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could we turn into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Higgins, we had some additional time yesterday to look at the video. The Chamber most likely will come with a decision on admission after the first break, but we have not thoroughly discussed the matter yet. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. I perhaps already make an observation in relation to an issue that -- well, came to the surface yesterday. This Chamber has heard quite some evidence about columns of people leaving the Krajina. If a column is shown on a video, whether or not it will be admitted, or if a burning house is being shown on a video, in the context of the evidence the Chamber has heard, the Chamber is not greatly assisted by a lengthy debate on whether these houses, in Sector North or Sector South, because if the one house shown would be in Sector North, that does not necessarily invalidate all of the evidence about burning houses in the south so, to that extent, whether it is exemplary or not is even not of great relevance, and, of course, Ms. Frolich one could wonder why this Chamber is presented with pictures of burning houses. We have seen quite a lot of them and to look at them in a different story again and again certainly is not of great assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was just to explain again, I was merely portraying these images just to make it more easy to understand what the witness was talking about when statements were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I hope you're not underestimating the intellectual capacity of this Chamber to know what a burning house looks like. To visualize that is after having been now for such a long time in court dealing with these matters is -- well, might not be the best use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and your examination will now be continued by Ms. Frolich for a short period of time and after that cross-examination will follow. Please proceed, Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could the last segment of the video be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Frolich give us an exact reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were invited to give a precise reference as where to start in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. -- this is page 17:33 in English, and page 16, line 29 in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: "Franjo Tudjman: The Croatian army never committed arson or destruction. People were saying that the whole of Knin went up in flame. I came to Knin and others came to Knin, and Knin was not burning despite the fights and the resistance, there was limited damage. "Alain Forand: We are also finding bodies as we go to a small village on a daily base. People that have been shot or people that have been their head, you know, cut. So what type of life can they expect by staying here? "Zarko Puhovski: We are talking about here about a large number of incidents which were influenced by motions. But these incidents, these motions had been prepared for years through propaganda, from television to the president of the country and all public factors in Croatia who convinced the Croatian population and especially the soldiers that the Serbs are guilty as such and that they should be punished as such."

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, good morning. Could you provide us with a few examples of the years of propaganda that you mentioned in this segment.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about it much like any other Croatian citizen could have at that time. Once the war began, Croatia was in a situation in which the general opinion that the Serbian attack was directed at undermining the Croatian state and the Serbs were supposed to prove their loyalty to be able to remain in their apartments and properties. We, in the Croatian Helsinki Committee received hundreds of such reports to that effect. At the same time, Serb literature and books were being taken out of public libraries, on occasion that included Russian books as well. On TV one could repeatedly hear statements in which there is no mention of the Yugoslav army, rather that army was usually referred to as the Serb army or the Chetnik army as the principal enemy of the Croatian state. It was present in the minds of many, including those in the army, in which they simply saw, as I said in the footage, the Serbs as a collective enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a point of clarification. Yesterday at page 64 of the -- yesterday's transcript, you were asked by General Cermak's position, where you said your knowledge came from three sources. I believe you did not finish your explanation. My question is, to your knowledge what was General Cermak's exact title and position in August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew that from various conversations with my colleagues who visited Knin and through my conversations with Mr. Pasic, as well as the media. All three sources refer to Mr. Cermak as the person who was in charge of deciding about things in Knin. Most frequently, he was referred to as the commander of Knin, or the boss. Whoever you talked to, they all referred to Cermak as the person who decides on what is going on in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. And just one item, for the record that video film, it was played is 65 ter 7049. Thank you. And if this -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In its entirety? Or just the portions, are they separated from ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No, the entirety of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The entirety of the video. Has a number already been assigned to the video as a whole? I just don't remember. Madam Registrar, has a number been assigned to the video?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The number hasn't been assigned to 65 ter 7049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please do that, and it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit number P2321, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Higgins, you will be the first one to cross-examine Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Higgins. Ms. Higgins is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind taking the microphone closer to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I'm going to start by asking you a few questions about your involvement in the Croatian Helsinki Committee for human rights, and for purposes of consistency for the record I'm going to try to refer to the organisation as the HHO. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand, the organisation was established in 1993 and from its inception until 1999, the president or the chairperson was Ivan Zvonimir Cicak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And from the period of 1993 to 1998, for the record, you acted as his deputy. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not throughout the period. I was his deputy as of 1994, and ending with 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You resigned in May of 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the deputy president, I resigned in 1997, and I left the committee all together in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification, and I'm going to come on a later stage to deal with your resignation. When did you go back to the HHO, after you had left?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And between the time of your resignation and the time you went back to work in June 2000, did you stop working for the association altogether in that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time, I spent three days every week in Austria. I was in charge of a graduate course. For purely physical reasons, I was unable to participate in their activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that during the time that you worked for HHO you were based in the office in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now in relation to events in the Krajina, I think it's right to say, is it, that Mr. Cicak was dealing with matters in Sector South? Is that right? That was one of the remits of his work?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was such that we did not have sectors I stood in for him when Operation Storm began. It just so happened that I was literally the only committee member in Zagreb. It was early August when most of the people are on the coast. Mr. Cicak was on the island of Brac. Our communication was interrupted and for the first ten days, I was doing everything from Zagreb because simply there was no one else. At that time, GSMs were infrequent. And on certain days you could you not establish any link. In the first ten days or so, I undertook all of the activities. After that, Mr. Cicak returned and then he was in charge of the activities as the president, including the activities pertaining to Krajina. Of course, I would stand in for him when he was under different or other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The transcript correction, Your Honour, at line 11 of page 8, it states that we did not have sectors. I'm informed it should say we did not have resources for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Higgins the procedure is that you say that there is a mistake. We ask then the witness to repeat the words, and not so that you give the right translation, but if it is not --

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not believe that is correct. I was listening to the witness in B/C/S, and I -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's then ask the witness what he said. Ms. Higgins, it was at --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Line 11 of page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you said: "The situation was such that you did not have ..." and then you continued by saying, "I stood in for him when Operation Storm began." Now, what did you not have?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no division in terms of sectors or remits or work, rather than territorial sectors. He as the president was in charge of all of the activities of the committee, and I was his deputy, within the same scope, same remit when he was unable to perform his function. Therefore, there were no separate remits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Higgins, this proofs how right the procedure is we adopted as a standard. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just out of interest, are you able to assist with who wrote the Sector North section of the report, the 2001 report that you're producing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire report, both North and South is something that was drafted by those who collaborated with Mr. Mrkalj. He decided on the final version of the text was published in 1999, and I double-checked it when it was supposed to be published as a book, and I added the text that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now you are one of two responsible editors for what I'm going to refer to as the Storm report so that we know that we're talking about the 2001 report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have recollection of when you started and ended your work as editor on that particular Storm report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been between late 2000 and the beginning of February 2001. I cannot be any more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you some more detail about the report. And I understand that given your role as editor, there may be parts that you are not able to help me with. So if that is the case, please, don't hesitate to indicate that, and I can then try and ask somebody else or find the information elsewhere, Mr. Puhovski. In your statement that you made to the Court, we know that the Storm report was based in large part on the HHO's fact-finding missions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, again, in your statement, you separate out those missions, as having taken place in mid-August 1995; September 1995; and March or April 1996. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We also know from the information that you've given, that in relation to the mid-August period, from your supplementary information sheet, a mission began on the 10th of August and lasted for three days. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In respect of the time-frames of September 1995 and March/April 1996, are you able or not to assist me with the precise dates of the fact-finding missions that took place?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, Mr. Cicak was back in charge. I am absolutely certain that there was a mission or, rather that there was a team that returned around the 10th of April, 1996. At that time Mr. Cicak was abroad, and I had a debriefing with them upon their return.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But just to clarify, in relation to the supplementary sheet where you stated that there were 10 to 12 returns to the area, I understand that you're not in a position to give me the exact dates. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You can't give me the dates?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot provide you with any precise dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the original reports, as I understand from what you've said, when a fact-finding mission goes down to the area, those members draw up a written report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Would it be one of the members, or all of the members who contributed, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the practice was, and -- as far as I know it was always applied. On our return to Zagreb, all of us would take a day's break, and then would come back for a meeting with our own notes. Each and every one of us had their own notes made from the field trip. Then each of us would -- we would be making the reports for each of the groups, and then Mr. Mrkalj would be going through all of these draft reports, unless the report had to do with the field trip that he was part of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Those original fact-finding mission reports from the Krajina period that we've discussed, where are those reports; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, a few of them are in the office of the HHO in Zagreb and some of them are in possession of the son of late Mr. Mrkalj. His name is Jadranko Mrkalj. He also talk part in some of these missions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Have any of those reports been provided to this institution, the ICTY, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any of the original reports were provided. I am not privy to that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And, again, given the level of detail you're able to help me with, are you in a position to tell me about the precise location of each fact-finding mission, or about the exact members who were party to each mission, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that in the first mission which was partly our mission and partly the mission with the International Helsinki federation, come priced of Mr. Petar Mrkalj and Ms. Petra Klein. The 10th of April mission had to do with the area of Hrvatska Kostajnica and it was Jadranko Mrkalj, Bozica Ciboci and Petar Mrkalj who were part of that mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So in respect of the ten other missions or so, you can't help me. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assist you with the exact dates or names. I can only tell you who the team of the people was, who participated in it. But I can't tell you when specifically which of these people took part in which of the missions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, we'll come on to this. But, again, as I understand from your evidence, the only part of the Storm report that you wrote were the three pages which you were shown in examination-in-chief, which are titled: Conclusion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you didn't write any of the fact-finding mission reports that underlay this storm report itself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because I did not participate in the missions, and it would not have been proper for me to write about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We'll come to that, your participation. Just dealing with this other point, if you can help me, were any of the original notes of the fact-finding missions ever translated into English, or do they remain in Croatian only?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost positive that nothing was translated into English, or at least I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And to establish at the outset, again, it would be right to say that, in terms of your involvement in the field, you were in Knin for a matter of a couple of hours. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the individuals who would go on the fact-finding missions, and I think it's right to say that would include Petar Mrkalj, Jadranko Mrkalj, Bozica Ciboci, Ranko Hellebrandt and Olga Simic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Hajdi Kadenec.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I know that Petar Mrkalj was trained as a journalist. Are you able to help me with the professions of the other members who would go out into the field on mission or not.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time his son Jadranko Mrkalj was a student Bozica Ciboci and Ranko Hellebrandt were student too. Olga Simic and Hajdi Kadenec were lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now again, just for the purposes of clarification, and I'm not interested so much as why, but as a fact, none of the documentation that came from those fact-finding missions was stored on computer or computer data files. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. The great majority was stored on a computer. It was a personnel computer belonging to Mr. Mrkalj. This was the case because of the reasons I stated yesterday, and that's the penetration of the military secret service into the HHO office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: At paragraph 5 of your statement, you refer to the fact that in relation to the accounts that were collected, again, concerning the Krajina, to use your words "there was no official way of checking the accuracy of the facts through the police." Is that a fair representation of what you have said in your statement and what you understood to be the case?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was most certainly the case in the first months that followed. When it was practically almost impossible to have any contacts with the official bodies. Eventually contacts with official bodies grew in intensity and improved. The practice was that it was necessary to go back to the same location twice or three times to see if anything changed, and in time, let's say in 1997 and 1998, the contacts were pretty normal, whereas back in 1995 and 1996 they were practically non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just continuing with the Storm report, 2001, again, as I understand from having read your statements, the precursor to this book was the report that was published on the 8th of April, 1999, and titled report: Operation Storm and subsequent events. Correct? You're nodding, but if you could indicate a yes for the record, please, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in your supplemental information sheet you provide the information that Petar Mrkalj wrote the entire April 1999 report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is certain is that he edited the entire text. I'm not sure how things went exactly. I wasn't in Zagreb at the time. What I know from my conversations with him and other colleagues, he practically re-edited the entire text because reports came in from individual journeys that were made, and he formulated it finally into the version that was circulated in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, you have described his task as a re-editing of the entire texts. Are you able or not to assist me with who wrote -- who were the authors of that 1999 report? Can you help with that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The same individuals who participated in the fact-finding missions in the field; namely, Jadranko Mrkalj, Bozica Ciboci, and others, all of them wrote their reports and on the basis of them, Petar Mrkalj drafted the final text.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to seek clarification of one other point which has become slightly disjointed through the service of your statement and supplemental notes so that I'm clear about it. In the first supplemental note that we received, it was stated there that you had written the conclusion of the Sector South part of the 2001 report. As I understand, from the second note that was given to us, it was stated that, again, you wrote the conclusion of the Sector South part of the report in 2000. Correction was made to that, and, again, it now seems to be the case that you wrote an introduction, as you have seen, to the Sector North part of the report, that we've already looked at. Do you recall seeing that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Let me repeat again. This is the text that I wrote for the purposes of the Croatian Helsinki Committee on the occasion of the fifth anniversary of Operation Storm which was subsequently added into the copy that was printed as a book ultimately. This particular text does not specifically refer to either Sector North or Sector South but to the situation that had arisen in the general area as of the result of the action.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I have looked very carefully at what you have written, Mr. Puhovski. I wonder if you could help me with this: In the piece, which may be perhaps be better phrased as an essay. You don't actually cite any footnotes or references. Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason is the book itself. The whole book is a footnote to the text, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Before the publication of the 2001 Storm report, was there any peer review of the book or the underlying reports? And by that I mean was the report sent out for review by other similar bodies to review the way in which it was compiled and the methodology used. Do you know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the 1999 text which is the basis of the book since the differences are really negligent, if we put aside my text, was sent to someone 150 addresses from state agencies to international organisations and embassies. We had the institute for migration, for sociology that looked at the text, between four and five university professors, political sciences experts, and several colleagues from Belgrade and Sarajevo also looking at the text, and I'm referring to the first version, dating back to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now in respect of that 1999 text, I know that it was distributed, and you have referred to the agencies there. But was it distributed before it was published for comment on its methodology at all?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question, since I repeat, I did not take part in the process. I only know of the consultations that took place between the publication of the photocopied version and the book itself. And I have given you my answer on that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Mr. Puhovski. Thank you. Going back to your travel to Knin, could you help me with, firstly, the dates of your travel, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can. I think it was the 12th of August, because in two or three days time, it was necessary to organise the arrival of the group of representatives from the International Helsinki Federation. Again I went there and stayed there for a couple of hours because the information we received from domestic media were different from the information divulged by the international media. We wanted to see whether they were able to go there at all. Some of our colleagues from the International Helsinki Federation were quite concerned because of the information they had received from Vienna. I believed it incumbent upon me to check up on that information. I repeat I was the only one in Zagreb at the time, and the general belief was that it wouldn't have been an easy job for either Mr. Banac or Mr. Cicak to make a journey from the islands where they were, the island of Brac, to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you think it was the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 12th, yes. But I'm not 100 percent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, conduct interviews with individuals on that date?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to several civilians in the UN base, in the UN compound. That could not be termed as a proper interview. I simply wanted to get an idea of what the atmosphere was like. And then I had a ten-minute or at least under half an hour conversation with Petar Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In relation to the conversation that you had with Petar Pasic, did you make any notes about that conversation at the time as a fact-finding mission member?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the mission. I simply wanted to check whether it was safe for the mission to arrive there, and I did not take any notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you also visit the police station when you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall who you spoke to there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to three or four policemen who were there. I don't know their names. They were not higher-ranking officers. They were ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You didn't meet with Mr. Cermak on that day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn back now to aspects of the fact-finding mission before we go and look in further detail at the report. You have mentioned, and we have discussed, the names of the fact-finding mission members. Did the students who took part, that being Jadranko Mrkalj, Bozica Ciboci, and Ranko Hellebrandt, receive any formal training as to how to conduct themselves on a fact-finding mission for a NGO? And I mean formal training.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't. At the time there was no realistic possibility to organise such a formal training. There was no practice to draw upon. As I said earlier, we tried to formulate the experience we had had and to train them during these weekend trainings. But these were people who basically had to learn as they went along, through their work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, I know from your supplemental note you say that the fact-finding team always asked the same questions about the details of witnesses and victims and the crime in question, as well as about the locations of units in the area. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, and that is true. After the first of such missions, sort of questionnaire was compiled on the basis of the experience drawn from the first mission, and subject to slight modifications that were made it, all the people who went on subsequent missions stuck to the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, do you have a copy of that questionnaire, Mr. Puhovski, yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I must have had it somewhere, but I misplaced it. It can be found in the archive of the Croatian Helsinki Committee in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you know whether that questionnaire was ever provided to the Office of the Prosecution in the conversations that took place between the HHO and the Office of the Prosecution? Can you help me with that or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days of the Tribunal, a group of two or three representatives of the Prosecution came in 1997, I believe. At the time, Mr. Cicak and I provided them with a copy of the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. Now I know, again, that you were only present for a couple of hours, and if you're not able to help me, please, just say so. But do you know from the conversations that you had with the fact-finding members who would return, whether or not it was one individual who conducted the interviews, or whether all members of the team would conduct interviews for whatever reason? Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. When Petar Mrkalj was on the team, he was always the one conducting the interview, or if he was not there, then any one of the members of the team would conduct the interview, depending on how they felt and depending on the composition of the team.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of a NGO, I understand, given that it was created in 1993, it would be fair to say that it was a relatively young institution by 1995. What I want to ask you about are the procedures that were or were not in place by 1995. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The committee was set up by people who had had experience from earlier human rights committees, Mr. Budak, Mr. Cicak, and I set up a human rights committee in 1989 which was the first such committee. Earlier on, in 1984 we were in the Croatian subcommittee to the Yugoslav Helsinki Committee. It was a semi-legal organisation, to put it that way. So we were able to keep afloat, as it were in such activities and we were able to convey that experience onto our colleagues. Undoubtedly the Croatian Helsinki Committee as a NGO, was only a two-year-old toddler at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: My question is very specific, and it relates to the interviews that were recorded with individuals on the fact-finding missions. It's my understanding that those interviews, in relation to those, the procedure was that they would be audio-recorded with a tape recorder at that time. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the case on the first mission, I'm sure about that, and I'm almost certain that all the other missions were taped. At the same time, members of the team would also be taking notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So what we have are apart from the first mission, we have audiocassette recordings, and we have some notes by the members. It wasn't, is it right to say, part of the procedure, at that stage, that those notes and audio-recordings would be made into a form of witness written statement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So to follow on from that, at that time of the operation of the HHO, there was no written record that was taken back to the individual to be verified and signed. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Forgive me if I asked you this question earlier on, but if you could just assist with me on this: Were any of those audiocassettes or notes handed over to the Prosecution, or were they retained - I think you said - by Petar Mrkalj's son, split between there and the HHO archive. Could you just clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that any of the material was provided to the ICTY Prosecution. The better part of it, at least until a couple of years ago, was in possession of Petar Mrkalj's son, who asked for a hefty sum of money from the Croatian Helsinki Committee in order for the committee to get a hold of that material. We believed it unnecessary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you know -- and again, you may not know given your role. But do you know whether, for example, on each and every interview that was conducted, the amount of time taken to interview and the location of interview, were they points that were recorded in either the audio or the notes, or are you unable to assist me with the entirety of that question?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that in the cases where I participated, in terms of debriefing, the colleagues who had visited the field always had precise data on where, when, and who spoke to whom. It was always in their written notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Along with the members of the fact-finding missions, were they ever accompanied by experts, such as forensic pathologists, ballistics experts, any one of that nature. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that no one accompanied them, ever. Those -- such missions would require additional five to six people who would be willing to go in the field, and I believe experts are not necessarily always the bravest of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Moving from the fact-finding mission to the report for a moment, the 2001 report, are you able to tell me whether or not there exists a list or a bibliography or an index, in whatever form, of all the sources that were relied upon to compile that 2001 report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing beyond the report exists in any formal shape. Anything that is outside the reports are the written notes and audiotapes, mostly in the possession of Mr. Mrkalj, as well as the references mentioned in the footnotes, and those that can be found in the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, just to conclude this section, would it be fair to say that given your absence from the field, you're not able to help me or the Court with any certainty, as to the accuracy of the actual process of recording information that was obtained from individuals, the process that was employed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I can tell you what I learned from the colleagues who returned from the field. They provided extensive reports on what they were doing, and, at that time, as today, I found it to be reasonable, under the circumstances. They try their best to convey the -- what they had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, I would ask that a bundle be distributed which I have compiled to try and assist both the Chamber and the witness in terms of speeding up the process of going through what is a rather long report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I can explain, Mr. Puhovski, for your benefit and for the Bench, this bundle is divided into section A, and you'll see a tab later on, section B. I'm going to take you through both of those. And you will see that there are tabs dividing which I hope will assist to us go through this relatively quickly. These are, of course, extracts from the 2001 report. And, again, what I'd like to do is take you to certain sections and draw to you my concerns that I would like your assistance with, if you're in a position to help me, with the proviso, please say if you can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So if we can go straight away to tab 1 in part 1, part -- section A, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, for e-court purposes, in English it is page 28, and in Croatian it stretches over pages 26 to 27, the report being 65 ter 4674. Your Honour, while that is coming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- you're referring to e-court paging?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- and hard copy in English, apparently starts at page 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed on the basis of the hard copy and not wait for the upload on to the screen, to save time. I will, of course, cite the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you deem appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Page 26 of the report, Mr. Puhovski, deals with -- you can see it has been highlighted so that we all know what we're talk being. You see the highlight section there. It deals with incidents concerning the shelling in part of Donji Lapac, an area which we know, for the record, to be outside the Split Military District. But the question I have for you, is if you look at the footnote, footnote 25 which supports the third paragraph there of the report, the interviewee is referred to by initial TK. Now, first of all, from the report itself and what you've seen, are you in a position or not to assist me with who the interviewer was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the interviewer. During that time, I did not take part in the debriefing process.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you know who TK was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who TK was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And for the purpose of comprehensiveness, in the second paragraph up from the bottom, 12 lines up in the English there is reference there to a line which starts: "According to the diary report of BA from the village of M ..." Can you help me with either of the references as to what they refer to, who BA was, what village M was, please, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Highlighted version here refers to the shelling of Knin. I'm not going to take you through the entire text, as we're all familiar, or can be made familiar with the text itself. Second line, you see reference to KS. Can you help me with KS's identity, or are you not in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you who it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, that is e-court English 29, Croatian 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If could you turn over the page, please, now to the second page of that tab, page 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, this is e-court English 30, Croatian 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom there at footnote 28, there is reference to this individual, KS, giving a statement to CHC activists. But we see that the date what is used is in fact the 11th of February, 1995, which we all know must be an error, given the timing of the incident at first.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original, it is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simply a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, that's helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we could go to tab 3, please. E-court English 31, Croatian page 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Fifth line down, in that paragraph, there is an account given by a disabled elderly woman. Can you assist or not can with the identity of that person, or when that interview was recorded, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about either of the things.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 4, please. E-court English 37, Croatian 35 to 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This section refers to Donji Lapac again, supported by a reference at footnote 4 by an individual ZL, called J, born in 1928, Donji Lapac. I presume from your answer, you're not able to assist me in relation to the identity of that individual. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the debriefings we did not touch upon the issue of names, because we believed at the time it was wise for as little people to be -- as few people to be familiar with the names as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Puhovski. Could I ask you, on that page, the paragraph that starts: "At least 38 persons ..." If you track through to the third line of that paragraph, it refers to: "The witnesses saw him ..." Track down to the second to last line: "The witnesses state ..." Any further detail that you have as an editor of this report that may assist this Court as to their identities, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we did however check and establish that Mr. Milan Medic could be seen on TV and that he was killed. I personally confirmed that when checking it with the -- in the archives. As for the other witnesses, I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm not trying -- just to be clear with you, I'm not challenging that fact. What I'm interested in is the underlying reference, just so that you and I are not in dispute over that. You will also see there in the second-to-last paragraph from the bottom reference to an incident concerning what's referred to as the old man Savo Bursac. Is there, to your knowledge, an identifiable source for that information, please, or can you not assist me with that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Bursac, we received a that information from the Red Cross. I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So the footnote there should be to a Red Cross report of some sort, I presume, should it? If there were to be one?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so. I did this verify with the family. They requested information, and they did indeed obtain information from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 5, please, which is e-court English 39, Croatian spreading over pages 37 to 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, same exercise. Refers to Knin. Please look at the footnotes 8 and 9. The identifiable source is referred to as NR, born in 1933, and KS. If you'd like to check your version, please, do so.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to tell you the same thing. I am not familiar with the initials. I may have known who the people were, but I have forgotten in the meantime. Whereas for most of the initials, I didn't know who they pertained to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 6, please. E-court English 41, Croatian 39 to 40. Events in Oton.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: References in footnotes 15 and 16 to VP and MK. Again, if you would like to check your text, please do so.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The response, unfortunately, is the same. I don't know who this pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let me skip very quickly through the rest of section A because I suspect we may be on the same ground here, Mr. Puhovski. Tab 7, please, English 43, Croatian 41. Footnote 21, in support of that paragraph that is highlighted concerning people who died in Mokro Polje, there is a reference to witness BA. Are we on the same ground here, Mr. Puhovski, that you can't help me with the identity?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The other point here is from the reading of the text, it doesn't appear clear as to whether or not the individuals -- the witnesses saw the killings or were told about them afterwards. Do you have any clearer information on that aspect of this paragraph, or are you not in a position to assist?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only help you by stating that, in principle, we only published the names or initials in the cases for which we had witnesses who had either witnessed the murders themselves or saw the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 8, please. E-court English 44, Croatian 42 to 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's this -- this page here, tab 8, the footnote refers to, in footnote 25, BA, as the witness in respect of these events. What I would seek is -- is, of course, the identity and/or the date of interview, if you know or can help.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 9, please. E-court English 45, Croatian 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Footnotes 26 and 27, witnesses BA and KL, to events described on that page. Any assistance or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same response.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 10. E-court English 47, Croatian 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Footnotes 32 and 33, individuals referred to as RD, KD. Is it the same response for that tab as well, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 11. English 54, Croatian 52 for the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, this tab, Mr. Puhovski, if you would like just to leaf through it, it actually extends to eight pages of the report. And it covers incidents relating to Grubori, Gosic, and Varivode. And if you look at that section of the report, the only individuals who have provided the source information are witnesses who are referred to as ZU, VZ, RD, KA, KS, along with an interview by Alun Roberts. Do you know the identities of these people or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 12, please. E-court English 61, Croatian 58 to 59.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Section entitled: Missing persons. Again, we've got reference here. If you leaf through, can you take it from me, if you like, Mr. Puhovski, but if you leaf through that section, the references are, again, to individuals by initial of SD - that's on page 60, middle of the page - NS, similarly, middle of the page, page 61, top of the page, ND. Same question, Mr. Puhovski, whether you know the identities or not of the individuals cited in this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Tab 13, please. E-court English 87, Croatian 83.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sources here, again, over the next couple of pages, you can take it from me that the sources are of the highlighted paragraphs BA, MH, and on page 87, an anonymous soldier. Same question, Mr. Puhovski: Can you assist, do you know or not? I have to repeat, we believed it was important to protect the witnesses, and not even committee members knew of their name, save for the ones who spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all background noise, especially typing be brought down to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Final example in this clip, tab 14, footnote 1, over the page, the second page of that tab for e-court, that's English 108 to 109. Croatian 104 to 105. We see again an initial KS. Can you assist with whether or not that's the same as the previous KS or not, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: KS, it is the same interview. It is the same date in 1999. I'm certain that's the same person, although I don't know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to continue through section B. I don't know whether Your Honour would like to take an early break or for me to continue with this exercise until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered whether this is a very efficient way of proceeding. If you would have prepared a list of footnotes, initials, and asked the witness to review over the break whether he could assist us in identifying the persons that would have saved I think some 70 per cent of the time spent on it in Court at this moment. And then of course you could have further given a follow up if there would be a positive response, but to listen for a half an hour that the person is not able to identify the persons mentioned by their initials only in the report is not -- I'm hesitant to say this, because I can't say that your Defence team is usually taking more time than one would expect, perhaps even on the contrary. I'm not commenting on that, but it explains my hesitation. Is there any way of -- of doing it in this way so that we can move on and not need half an hour to establish that the witness is unaware of the persons hidden behind these initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of section B of this document, I must say for the record that it actually took considerable time to try and think of the best way to not only just cite a list but to give this witness a fair opportunity of reviewing what I'm referring to, and I have tried to assist everyone by compiling it in this way, and I know Your Honour will understand that. But for section B what I propose is, if I, over the break, allow Mr. Puhovski to review section B, I can deal with it very shortly on my return, perhaps within the space of five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it then that Mr. Puhovski is invited to look specifically at the highlighted portions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication whether the same questions is to identify persons that are given initials in these portions. Is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of section B is actually unfootnoted, unsourced passages of the report. So the question is different but a slight variant in the sense of can Mr. Puhovski assist or not. The examples are then there for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, assist in identifying --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the source of this portion of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I'm hesitant to ask you to do some homework over the break. However, if you would be willing, and I know it's 19 tabs, but to briefly review the highlighted portions under tab B and see whether you can add anything to the report, in terms of the identity of the source. That's what we're talking about, isn't it, Ms. Higgins?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could deal with this in the most efficient way after the break. I further would like to inform the parties that there are still some submissions to be made where the Chamber said Thursday or Friday, that I take it that the parties are aware of -- of what I'm talking about, and the Chamber would like also to know whether the parties have any issue with making the Prosecution motion we are talking about and it's Appendix C, a public document. That's the first question. And whether there's any problem there making the Gotovina Defence response a public document as well. If you would please would conclude that. We'll hear -- Mr. Waespi, we'll hear your submissions by the end of today's session. That is ten minutes for each party, so we'll start a little bit before 1.30. Then we will we have a break. Mr. Puhovski, I'm sorry to ask you to do some extra work. And we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I would need to address a few matters very shortly, so my apologies for -- and I'm asking for your patience. First of all, P2321, MFIed, is 65 ter 7147, and not as appears on the record this morning, 7049. That's a correction to the -- Then the Chamber has decided that the documentary film, Storm Over Krajina, is admitted into evidence in full. However, I immediately add and want to emphasize that a large portion of that film has, if any, not much probative value. I think I hinted already this morning at events where we do know where it is, we do not know who it is, so that is emphasised by the Chamber, that major portions are, as said, if not at all, without much probative value. At the same time, it's very practical. I mean, to ask the Prosecution remove burning houses, to remove running soldiers, to remove landscapes with piles of smoke, that is -- is a huge effort, and even without it being removed the Chamber is able to consider what the probative value is or, perhaps more important, what -- where there is hardly, if any, probative value in that. We do not want to have this whole film re-edited. That doesn't make sense. So the parties should understand that the admission of the video in its entirety does not mean that the Chamber would consider the -- most of it to have significant probative value. Then there's another matter, but I'll leave that until, at the end of today's session. Ms. Higgins, perhaps we inquire whether the witness whether he was able to review the tab B documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, did you have an opportunity to look through section B of the clip that I provided to you in the break?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The purpose of me providing you with that clip was to bring out examples of the report where there are no footnotes which support the sections, in terms of sources, for those parts which are highlighted, and I'm sure you understood that as we -- just before the break as I tried to clarify what the documents related to. Are you in a position to help in providing any detail in respect of those passages, or not, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report from a non-governmental organisation, which was made public and contained information that the NGO was able to obtain. This was not made for the purposes of a court or anything else but for the sake of the public, which is what is stated in the foreword to the book. I can tell you in the past in the ten years of its incomplete publication and the eight years of it's official publication, none of the facts contained therein were called into question. Save for one piece of information which we managed to confirm being true. This is what I can tell you, generally speaking. We did not consider it our duty to come out with information about our sources. Quite the contrary. We believed that that might threaten their safety. In a number of situations our activists engaged in field work, submitted reports to us that we made public as -- in the form in which they were, and that's the only thing I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, your report is being produced now in a criminal trial, and it's for that reason, which I know you understand, that I have to ask you about the underlying material, and I take your answer, and I'm going to ask you now to move on, and to look at -- I'm going to ask you questions about the three annexes at the back of that report, which I know you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the purposes of e-court, that's English, starting at 138, Croatian, starting at 132.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, to shorten this part of the process, Annex 1 refers to civilians killed during and after Operation Storm, as you will recall; Annex 2 refers to terrorism and violence incidents; and Annex 3 refers to abuse.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the purposes of the Bench, annex 1 starts at hard copy page 137 and then continues through.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: At the start of Annex 1 concerning civilians killed during and after Operation Storm, you state -- or, rather, the report states at the end of paragraph 1 that at the time of publication the list, it says, is not final. Do you see that at paragraph 1 of Annex 1?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now none of these Annexes, and I'm going to take them generically, cite how the organisation obtained the details in respect of each of the individuals listed here, and you will, of course, note the relative brevity of what is recorded in this, as you have called it, the NGO report. Can you assist me with any further level of detail or not, in respect of firstly how the organisation obtained the details for each person, or is that level of detail not something that can you deal with?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is to repeat what I said. The method was to have two independent sources and if they provided the same information, then it would be published. We had some 160 to some 170 names for which we could not obtain a confirmation from two independent sources, and these names were not published. Our activists had to verify information from two independent sources; namely, two witnesses, or institutions or organisations. We wanted to keep it as brief as possible, since the intention was to come out in the public with the names of those killed, rather than the numbers. We did not want to draw the attention of the public to the numbers as much as to the names of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I ask that document 2D09-0008 be uploaded on to the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: While that is coming up, can I provide some background for both yourself, Mr. Puhovski, and the Bench. This is a table that has been created by our Defence team on the basis of analysing Annex 1 of the report and studying data that comes from the Croatian government administration for detainees and missing persons. That data is relied upon in these tables and was published in something that you may well be familiar with, the title of which I had is the book of missing persons in the area of the Republic of Croatia, which was published in December 2006 by the ICRC. Are you familiar with that document published by the ICRC, Mr. Puhovski, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the review that has been conducted here, just so that you have the context, names have been looked at in Annex 1 of the 2001 report and a comparison has been made with information coming from the ICRC statements of the families looking for individuals, which was published in that text I referred to, in December 2006. For the purpose of the screen so that you've seen it, this document spreads to three pages. And as you can see the HHO number of the individual is in column 2, the names are then provided; and in the last column the status which refers to exactly the public document which has been used for the purpose of comparison. If we can scan over to the second page, please, and the third page, you'll see that the table actually refers to 17 different individuals. These individuals, Mr. Puhovski, were recorded as civilians who had been killed during and after Operation Storm in Annex 1, but were actually, when the comparison was done, you will see all of them were found in military uniform. Now my question for you is the following: Was ever such a comparison done between Annex 1 of the 2001 report and the ICRC data that was published in December 2006 by your organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was published five and a half years after the publication of our report. We received it from the Red Cross roughly six months before it was published. We found, and that was important, that the names of those killed were basically consistent, and that in the meantime, if you look at the autopsy reports most of the autopsies were done already after we had finished our report. And the fact that somebody is aged 55, like Mr. Petar Milic and was found in military uniform, well, this does not mean that this person was a soldier. It is common knowledge that there were people on both sides wearing a uniform, and nevertheless they were civilians on the run.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that after December 2006, when the ICRC data became public, the HHO did not review the 2001 report, in light of that data. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat, we received the report from them earlier on, before it was published, in summer -- in the summer, and we compared it against our data. As I said, in the majority of cases, the names were consistent, and this is what mattered to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So the fact that individuals were found in military uniform, you did not consider to be a relevant factor in determination of our Annex 1, in assessing Annex 1 of your report. Is that right? You discarded it as irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because -- no, we did not discard it as irrelevant. We took it into consideration. The book was already published by that time. However, we believed it was our primary task, and I -- I stated this at page 93 of the Croatian version, that we spoke of the military and civilian victims about which we received information. Some information indicated that certain individuals were civilians. And the fact that this report stated that they were found in military uniform was not that relevant. For 14 individuals, unless I'm mistaken, it was established that they were found naked, and the immediate conclusion was that whatever clothes could be got by were put on them before they were buried. Therefore, while it was not a confirmation of the fact that an individual was a civilian, it was neither a denial of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would seek admission of this table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have an objection. I would have two reasons. Firstly we would have to check the accuracy of the underlying document -- of the facts as stated in the underlying document. So therefore I would seek at least that the document would be MFIed at this moment, but also I believe the heading which says the list of persons for which the documentation showing that they are military formations members exists is misleading in the light of what is actually listed in the table, which is persons in military uniform, some of which are listed as soldiers but not all. So we would seek an amendment to that heading, and, of course, checking of the accuracy of the underlying facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, an amendment to the title will be undertaken by the Defence. I would seek one point of clarification. Of course, we can disclose this material, the underlying material, to my learned friend, but I wonder whether in fact they have it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I do believe we might all the material. If -- in fact, I cannot be certain at this point. I do believe we have it, but we will have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be very practical, I mean, of course, for admission, full accuracy is not -- and 100 percent reliability is not required. At the same time if there are any -- any mistakes which can be justified, that saves everyone one version in evidence and then the next version in evidence. Now about the title, Ms. Higgins, I would have a question there as well. Yes, you say errors about the status which seems to a conclusion that the errors are not made by the ICRC but by another. Wouldn't it be appropriate to talk about comparison between the data?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- then it's introduced in such a way that not conclusions are already in the title, and that -- of course, it wouldn't change anything for the Chamber, but I think it would be the appropriate way of presenting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely agree, and this is one of a series of four tables, so can I make an undertaking to review the titles of the -- of the documents which came to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm attempting to deal with that and, of course, I will undertake to do. To make it more reflective of what's actually stated in the table itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again, of course, the title you attach to a certain document, of course, we'll look at the substance of the document, rather than at the title, and, therefore, errors -- unless you meant that the ICRC made an error here or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... You didn't say who made the error. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with how you wish to proceed on this. I do wish to note, though, that inn terms of what the admissibility of this chart later, in terms of the argument that the OTP needs to check the underlying materials, I just wanted to note the irony of the fact that we're talking about a report that they've tendered that can't be checked because there are no underlying materials. Just in terms of the admissibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, I -- yes, I see your point, but, of course, Ms. Frolich is now responding to the underlying material which is presented in this report. And again there, Ms. Frolich, it's -- there's nothing against it. Whether it bears on admissibility but, again, if these matters are sorted out in an early stage, if there are any mistakes, if, for example, you say number GO 5/0323 B, that must be mistake, that saves the Chamber later from spending hours if not ages on trying to find this autopsy report. So it seems to be very practical. And Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I, therefore, given your observations ask the document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then replaced by another one. Madam Registrar, this document, which is not the final version, will be marked for identification under number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under number D1302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it is now on the record. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. If I could now call up 2D09-0014 on to the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: This is the second document, the second table in a series, Mr. Puhovski. And for the moment if you could ignore the title, and we will concentrate on the content of the document itself. It runs to two pages and takes 11 individuals from Annex 1. The information this time, again from the ICRC materials, relates to individuals who have been reported by their family members as soldiers of various units where it was possible to identify that. My question for you - and, again, if it can be turned over to the second page of the English. Mr. Puhovski has the entirety in Croatian - you will see the level of detail or not that is provided by the family statement in search of the individual. Now, again, the same question: When this data was published in December 2006, was a review -- or, rather, you had access to it before. Did you specifically consider the material contained in those Red Cross materials or not for the purposes of Annex 1?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat again. By the time Annex 1 had been published for five years, Nikola Olic, son of Drazan, was found in a Croatian uniform. He was definitely not a soldier and certainly not a soldier of the Croatian army. This is something that we established. But we did not use this piece of information to indicate that all the other information is wrong as well. We took it upon ourselves to establish the individuals who were victims, and we compared it against the book which had, by that time, been published for five years. There was no reason for a book that was already published and was already there for the public to be reworked on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So the short answer to the question is, yes, you reviewed the materials; and, no, it was not included. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The better part of it was not. For some of the things they were right, for the others we were right. Primarily it had to do with the clothing in which the victims were found. I repeat that I do not agree with the statements made in this report that the clothes indicated the persons were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I ask that that document be marked for identification, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: My objection would be the same as for the last one because the entry as for the heading of the table, entry number 10, person [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in military uniform. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Ms. Higgins has already announced that she would review the titles, so that is understood. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit D1303, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. When will we hear from you, Ms. Frolich, in relation to checking the accuracy of the sources that are presented in this comparative table?

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: I believe that by Monday we could have the accuracy check completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I have always problem in having the same -- several documents at the same time on my screen. To try to make it easy, the first one and second one, is that 17 plus 11, or is any overlap between them so the total number of persons were ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As I understand, Your Honour, and I just -- if you give me a moment, I just check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a slight overlap. The difference being that the first table that I presented is based on more documentation, a mixture of Prosecution evidence -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. What I'm asking for is whether we have all together 28 persons, or do we have 23, 24, or 17 or 18?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We'll give you the precise number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next table, please, is D209-0022.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, this table again with the same proviso as regards the title, provides by looking again at the ICRC material, further detail of the circumstances which are known of the individuals that died. These individuals are contained, for the Benches clarification, within tables 1 or 2, so they're not additional individuals, but more information is provided there. Mr. Puhovski, I have already asked you about consideration of this material. So I don't propose to address that further.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But I would seek admission of this document that it be marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, may I take it same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
