utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit D1304, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could you please inform the Chamber once the new versions have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The final table in this series is 2D09-0017. And for your purposes, Mr. Puhovski, the material from this table comes from Prosecution source material concerning autopsy reports and MUP sanitation protocols as well as ICRC information. All of these individuals from a comparison of those documents, it is indicated or apparent from the face of the collection of material that those individuals either died as a result of natural causes or suicide, as opposed to being killed within or after Operation Storm. Now, if you could cast your eye - and the document runs to three pages, please - and again tell me whether that information is familiar to you and your organisation, in terms of the three different sources and whether it was considered and/or any reference made in the report, as I couldn't find one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to the documentation of the ICRC, this is something that I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask that document as well to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Same position as previously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit D1305, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will keep that status. Ms. Higgins, one question. May I take it that the tables you have presented by now are the result of a systematic comparison, or does the Chamber have to go through the same exercise? It's not just examples, but it is what you could find on the basis of the materials that are available.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to verify that, as to whether it has been provided to me as examples or as an entirety of what could be find in relation to the entire annex. If Your Honour would permit me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will. So therefore the nodding yes on your right-hand side was premature.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, we'll wait and -- wait for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I now want to move away from the tables, and I'm going to ask you some questions about sections of the report that deal with Mr. Cermak. I know that you never met Mr. Cermak and that you never met with him when you travelled down to Knin. So, again, I want to be specific and I would like you to be specific, and I would like you to name, when possible, the sources of information that you rely upon, as I know you understand the context of this as a criminal trial. Do you understand, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, of course. Yesterday I talked about the fact that the reports are relied upon were based on the conversations I had with the colleagues who participated in the mission of the IHF in Knin, if you are referring to my report. The assessments or conclusions provided were the result of the work of those activists who were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to remind you, you cited three sources; one being the activists; one being Petar Pasic, who you spoke to in Knin; and the third one being General Cervenko from media report, from --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the report. That refers to the report, the third one, it's not my personal experience, personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's start backgrounds and deal with Mr. Cervenko first.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I ask that the page of the report be uploaded please. It's for hard copy purposes, page 82 for the Bench, and English version 84, page 84, Croatian, I am afraid, scans over pages 79 to 81.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you know what I'm referring to. And on that page, just as it's coming up on the screen, it's footnote 3. Now, I'm not going ask you about what Mr. Cermak was alleged to have said; you understand there has been a ruling about that. But I'm going to ask you about your reliance on a media source which is cited here, General Cervenko. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Our belief was based on the fact that interviews and texts were published which were not subsequently denied or contested. We believed those to be the facts that we can use in our report, and so we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Puhovski. Let's, for the record, just look at the extract itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's from a Nacional report on the 5th of November, 1997 at the bottom of footnote 3. It states: "Cervenko said it is not true that he was, in Knin, some kind of civil person." And we know that he is referring to Mr. Cermak from the passage slightly above. "These are rubbish. He was a military person. How can someone be a civil governor in military uniform with General's rank with the military units who support him. This is it simply funny." Do you see that? Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you ever come to hear in the media or anywhere else as to whether General Cervenko had actually ever stated that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we carried the quotation from Nacional in the report, and you have the date against which you can verify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: My question was whether it came to your attention as to whether Mr. Cervenko had ever denied saying that? Was there of a denial of that newspaper report, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me, I misunderstood. I know of no denial.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In that case, could I ask for 2D09-0006 to be brought up onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to wait so that you have the Croatian version, so that the Bench has the English version. This, Mr. Puhovski, is a newspaper article from the publication Vjesnik dated the 6th of November, 1997, headed: "Cervenko, I did not give an interview to Nacional." In that article before you, he states that not only did he not give the interview but that he denies the content and meaning of the statements imposed on him. He then goes on to say: "I confirm that I did not give this interview, and all that was mentioned in the article is nothing but a simple construction drawn out from one accidental and disjointed conversation that was secretly recorded by the reporter, and then its content and meaning were roughly twisted, and the reporter produced it as his answers and my alleged replies." He then explains: "I will request that the act of the reporter and editorial board which are unheard of be discussed at the counsel of the Croatian Media Association, said General Cervenko in his official denial." You never saw that, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did see the following issues of Nacional in which they were trying to prove that they were in possession of an audiotape to that conversation, and that the journalist association did not follow up on this request and did not discipline the journalist for unprofessional conduct. That is why I believe the data to be reliable that it could be published.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you did know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was discussion within Nacional itself. It would be natural to have a denial carried by Nacional. I didn't know of this denial. I did see, however, that Mr. Spanovic published in Nacional that he had a tape of that conversation that he would show to anyone who asked to. And he also stated that his home association did not discipline him for any unprofessional conduct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So your report didn't think it appropriate or fair to put the context of that quote that's cited properly, and the fact that the man who was alleged to have said it made an official denial. That wasn't something considered for your report? That what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat, the contents were confirmed by Nacional we were interested in the contents, not the format.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, there it is, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to move on. Could I firstly ask that that article be exhibited please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours the document will become Exhibit D1306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, did you come to know through any of your sources or contacts on this subject, before we leave it, that General Cervenko had in fact apologised to Mr. Cermak for any embarrassment this may have caused him, given its inaccuracy? Did that come to your attention or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. If we then work backwards, the second of your sources that you rely upon for the comment that you made that you were told by Mr. Pasic that Mr. Cermak was in charge, this was during a ten-minute conversation with Mr. Pasic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it lasted for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I think it's right that you said that you didn't have any notes of that conversation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I think it lasted between 20 and 30 minutes. That's what I said two hours ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Now, did you know that Mr. Pasic had made a statement to this Tribunal, a written statement? Were you aware of that in your research or work for the HHO?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask whether in the course of that conversation he addressed certain matters with you, and I'd like to take to you certain passages.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So could I ask that ICTY Prosecution statement of Mr. Pasic, which is 2D09-0029, be called up, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss with Mr. Pasic any specific cases because I wasn't familiar with any at the time. We were talking about the situation in Knin and about what was being reported from Knin at the time, as well as the atmosphere in town, which, to me, did not look like things were under control. On three our four occasions in the course of the discussion when we talked about that, he would say, Well, I have to discuss such matters with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to more generic questions about what you know about Cermak in a moment. What I'd like to do, please, first of all, is to ask you whether or not you and Mr. Pasic discussed certain matters. For that I'd like the English page 4 to be brought up onto the screen, please, of that document, and in B/C/S, that's page 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, can I just, for the record, state that this statement was taken, interviewers Brian Foster, Robert Casey, interview dated 22nd and 23rd of November 2001, March 2002, and the 3rd of March 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I do not know what questions will follow. But may I take it that these are questions that have been dealt with already without reference to the statement of another potential witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, given that this witness had contact with Mr. Pasic, I'd like to ask him whether he addressed certain issues or was informed of certain issues to put his comment into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you first ask him, and then if Mr. Pasic said anything similar or different, then, of course, I take it that you'll ask for an explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, the easiest way of doing this is perhaps if I rely on information that I have, and then you can tell me yes or no, whether or not those matters were discussed or comments made for the sake of efficiency. Did Mr. Pasic tell you that Mr. Cermak was in fact there in Knin to assist civil authorities. Was that something he mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that everything that had to do with normalizing things and civilian life in Knin had to go through General Cermak. I believe that is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... normalisation of life.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: He didn't tell you about Mr. Cermak's area of responsibility, did he? He talked to you about the general daily life in Knin. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat what I've just said, we didn't discuss any specific cases, since, at that time, I wasn't familiar with any. We only talked about what and how can be done in order to normalize the situation in Knin. And most of the more important questions were answered by him along the lines of, That's something we need to discuss with General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did he discuss with you anything concerning -- let me preface this by saying this: That part of the report deals with General Cermak either minimizing or denying crimes. There are references in the report there. Did Mr. Pasic tell you, for example, that General Cermak, that he was present with General Cermak, in daily meetings at the garrison and that General Cermak was angry about what had been going on concerning the crimes. Were you privy to information from Mr. Pasic on those matters or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat once again. I didn't discuss any crimes with Mr. Pasic because I had no names and information about any victims of crimes as something that I might be interested in as a member of the Helsinki Committee. We discussed things such as electricity, water supply, the police, road traffic, everything that had to do with the normalisation of life in Knin. I was there in order to see what the preconditions were for a visit of the IHF to Knin. At that time I had no information on any crimes that I could show anyone or request that someone be called to task about that, even if that had been my remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to just take you now to a line in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the Bench's purposes, the page is page 12, and for e-court English 14, Croatian 13. Your Honour, while that is coming up, I would seek the admission on the basis of the document which I have tendered concerning the ICTY statement of Petar Pasic to be admitted MFI at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it should only be applicable to the portions of which the witness has given some evidence, not the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that the content of the statement was put to the witness. I think you asked him questions, and upon my guidance you did not refer to his statement, but you said that you would rely on your own information. So, therefore I'm -- of course, I'm not in a position to -- but it's unclear to me what the purpose is of, at this moment, MFIing the document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In that case I would seek to take him to the passages to of Mr Pasic's statement which deals specifically with Mr. Cermak and to ask him about them. I was trying to shortcut the necessity to do so by abbreviating what I have got from the statement itself. But if my learned friend objects to, at this stage, it being MFIed, then I think I may have to go through the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, of course, I'm thinking about Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. That is the reason I have asked for it to be simply MFIed at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm always criticized by my staff to have a too long MFI list. And I'm just wondering that if for legal reasons we could shorten it. Ms. Frolich, could it be MFIed for the time being, and I think all lawyers in this courtroom are aware that statements taken for the purposes of proceedings before this Tribunal are not -- not easily admitted into evidence without all the requirements under Rule 92 bis having been met. I leave it at this moment to you, whether you -- if you want to confer with Mr. Waespi, then you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: There are no objections to the statement being MFIed at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please MFI the statement, assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit D1307, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Higgins, I take it that any point in time, we'll have further discussions on tendering and whether or not it should be admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the way in which we have been able to deal with this, it shortcuts the number of passages I would like to deal with, but nonetheless there are two that I'd like to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I'm going to read you a passage, and I'd like your comment on it. And I'm sorry if this will lead back to the same conclusion concerning normalization of life, but let me just read this to you: "For Mr. Pasic's statement, as far as I know, Cermak was there to assist the civil authorities. He would direct me to organise the feeding of people which took place where Cermak had his office, HV Dom, and he would push me to open the stores. Cermak had the logistics base and about ten or so soldiers under him. He also insisted that there be a public kitchen to feed the people who had no money. He wanted the civil authority to function so that he would not be bothered with the feeding of the people. Within a few days, we were able to get power and water functioning in the town." A passage, Mr. Puhovski, that again relates to normalisation and may ring in your ears or at least some of the content of that concerning normalization. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it correct. And to repeat, I only talked to Mr. Pasic about these things, save for two or three margin ideal details inquiring about some people that I had heard of wanting to learn of their fate. But at that time he was unable to answer those.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic stated: "I did not know Cermak's area of responsibility. I would meet with him every day. There was an agenda, and those items on the agenda would include, for example, an update on power supply, how to deal with the Serbs in the UN compound, security matters. Cermak would be asking what had been done on these issues, and people would respond. There were discussions about killings, lootings, and destruction. Often it would be Cermak who was telling us that these things were happening and asking what was being done about it. It would have been the internationals that would have reported these crimes to Cermak and myself at a different meeting. I remember that Gambiroza would often say that there were not enough policemen in Knin to cover such a large area." Part of the report, Mr. Puhovski, of course, relates to those in the UN compound with which you were familiar because you went down to Knin and visited that area. Is that right? I see you're nodding.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic stated, My belief was that the returning Serbs or those who had remained and the internationals did not trust the Croatian police to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, you're reading ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, too quickly. I am a getting carried away. I will refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes as long as you can take the transcriber with you, then there is not problem, but, if not, then you should adapt to her pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, I will amend the pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: "Cermak would ask what had been done, and he was very unpleasant to people and would shout at them if things had not been done. As far as the killings, looting, and destruction was concerned, he was not happy about it." One final passage, Mr. Puhovski: "At the meetings with the internationals, they would bring it up, the crimes being committed, and ask for more police action, and Cermak would say that there are just not enough men. The internationals wanted enough check-points to stop people who were not from the villages going there, and to stop the police patrols going there because the police were not trusted. I personally think that they did have enough police, and if they had done the job they should have done, a lot of the crimes would have happened." Now, Mr. Puhovski, have I asked you about the conversation. It was clearly a brief one. You have dealt with it with me, concerning what was discussed between Mr. Pasic and yourself. I'd like to now ask you several more questions, just about the point that's now on the screen in front of you, page 12 of that report. Do you see on the first paragraph, the last line. It states: "General Colonel Ivan Cermak was the military commander of Knin." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, underneath that passage, there is a list of units, forces, brigades, tanks which this report states took part in military operation in Sector South. Can you tell me - and again, I understand your role - but who was responsible for writing this unreferenced, unsourced piece of text? Can you help?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was most certainly written by Petar Mrkalj. That's beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your coming as the witness, so I'm going to ask you this question. When you visited Knin, you didn't know what Mr. Cermak's job was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I didn't know. When it comes to a formal function I only knew that he was the person everyone turned to. He was in charge, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, he may have been the person that people turned to for normalization of life, Mr. Puhovski, which is something very different from a generic responsibility. Your discussions that you have told us about concern his role in normalizing life. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this with Mr. Pasic. I was discussing with him who it was, who the International Helsinki Federation should be talking to when they come to Knin, and his response was, Of course, with General Cermak. And so they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And part of the reason as to why they did that was because General Cermak would speak to those organisations and would speak to the press. That was the information had you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic told me as follows: You have to let me know in time so that we can fit them into the schedule, because he is constantly being bothered by such-and-such a person. I think that this is how he put it, that there was always someone there, wanting to see General Cermak. He didn't specific say who, but I suppose it was journalists people from the country and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you know or come to know that there was in fact no such position as military commander of Knin, as is written here, at page 12?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall this correctly, it was only in 1997 that this matter was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And there was no information from either yourself or the HHO fact-finding mission members as to what resources he had available to him, was there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any information to that effect. The colleagues from the International Federation had already gathered some information by that time, and, as far as I know, they conveyed the information to General Cermak at their meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you or your colleagues know that he was in fact appointed as the Knin garrison commander on the 5th of August, 1995? Was that information you had?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, not by that title. That's the difference, Mr. Puhovski. The title I have used does not -- you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The function described in our text, in the Croatian, the term is military commander, so it has been translated correctly. That was the term colloquially used and widely used at the time by the media as well, in reference to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you or your colleagues have the information that he had a mere staff of nine individuals, from either your sources with Mr. Pasic or other members that were spoken to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic told me that there were only a handful of them or that there were -- there weren't enough of them, I don't remember exactly. But he was complaining about the fact that weren't enough of them there to run Knin. I didn't speak to him about police matters because did I go to the police station afterwards. I do recall him saying that a lot of the things were left uncovered, gaps were left where things could be happening, and I do recall him saying and repeating there's too few of us here, and I don't recall him specifically saying whether this included the police or not, or everybody put together, but I did not go into the matter since I was expected to go to the police station afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you know of any records, yourself, of any of the HHO staff members or fact-finding mission members having personally met with Mr. Cermak? Part of your knowledge or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the meeting with the International Helsinki Federation, I believe it was Mr. Cicak who had a meeting with Mr. Cermak, which transpired at a much later stage, in autumn, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Are there notes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there are any. If there are any, they can probably be found in the minutes because Mr. Cicak spoke about this at the meeting of our executive board of the HHO, in October or November of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you or any of your colleagues had the opportunity to review any of the extensive military documents which have been part of this trial and looked at what was actually sent to Mr. Cermak? Now it's a specific question. If you haven't, just please say so.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puhovski, part of your report also deals with the displaced persons in the camp. The extract that I'd like to just very quickly take you to starts --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the Bench purposes hard copy page 21. For e-court purposes, it's E 23 to E 24, Croatian 22 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again while that is coming on to the screen, let me say I'm not going deal with what Mr. Cermak stated or what is stated there about Mr. Cermak. But on that first page, there is reference to General Cermak on August the 20th, contacting the representatives at the camp. It's under number 3, and it's probably the third line down. If can you see that, Mr. Puhovski. Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you or your colleagues come to know in the research that you did you on Sector South, or the research that your fact-finding mission members did, that the assistance that Mr. Cermak gave to those displaced persons started way back, just after his appointment and is recorded in UN reports as far as back as the 7th of August in 1995, when he expresses a desire to meet with the refugees in the camp and the committee. Is that something you came to know or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at the camp, I heard that Mr. Cermak had been to see them. I wasn't told when that exactly happened. The people who were in a way taken carry of at the camp, as well as the UN personnel at the camp, said that the situation was quite all right within the camp itself but that was quite dangerous to venture outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, the document I'm referring to is P359. I'm not going to have it pulled up on to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Following on from that, Mr. Puhovski, did you come to hear that there was a subsequent meeting on the 8th of August where in fact measures were announced as to the rights that would be protected in respect of those displaced persons in the camp, including, for example, all civil rights and liberties, social security, settlement of pensions, provision of food. Did you know about the issuing of that particular document, or was something that didn't come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the Court's reference that's D300, the document that I'm relying upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you also come to hear through your contacts down in Knin that General Cermak had been there contact with General Forand on the same date asking for a list of refugees, specifically so that he could address their problems. Is that something you had come across?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of my visit to the camp, I learned that the Croatian side had asked for a list of refugees -- or, rather, the persons who were inside the camp. But I was not told what the reason for that list was, and I wasn't given an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That document is P388, again not to be called up on the screen. I know the Bench is very familiar by now with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to summarize, Mr. Puhovski, more meetings on the 10th, the 12th, and in fact a thank you letter that was sent out to Mr. Cermak on the 15th, thanking for him for the assistance he had given to those in the camp. Something you knew about or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the meetings. I didn't know the dates. And I didn't know about the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You also knew, did you, from perhaps what was in the report and what you had been told, that Mr. Cermak was giving assistance in terms of issuing passes, along with the MUP who were also issuing passes, which were also being handed out by Mr. Pasic, who we've spoken to. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of those days, I had a meeting with Minister Jarnjak who was the minister of the interior at the time, and he informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that the intention was to try and assist people to a get around the area and to facilitate them to getting access to their homes in what was nonetheless difficult circumstances at that time. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way. In my conversation with Minister Jarnjak and by that time around the 20th of August, I was already better informed. I asked him to his surprise that people not be released from the camp at the time, and that if they are released that they be escorted. We had information to the effect that people leaving the camp and going back to their villages were exposed to attacks. Minister Jarnjak told me at that time that what I was saying went against the interests of the people who wanted to go back to their homes. I told him something that was perhaps inappropriate of me, but I believed I had to tell him, and that was people are not aware of what is going on and you have to make sure that they stayed there for as long as they can. What I was telling him was based on the information I received about what befell the individuals who went out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Changing tack a little bit, Mr. Puhovski, if you would take it from me, as I think it may speed up the process, English page 83 of the report, hard copy page, can be put on to the screen as E, English, e-court 85, Croatian 82. There is an reference in the middle of that page to Mr. Cermak, stating that he did not report about atrocities that were occurring in the region under his command. Moreover he tried everything to cover up the incidents in public, justifying all that happened by emphasizing that it was the conflict with Chetniks, in one word he tried to minimise the whole problem. Were you or your colleagues aware of both reports to the UN and to the media of Mr. Cermak admitting that crimes were taking place or expressing his unhappiness about what was happening in the area? Did any of that come to your attention, Mr. Puhovski?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about some of these matters. We were referring here to something that can be seen in the documentary film, Storm over the Krajina. The Croatian television broadcast Mr. Cermak's statement who connected the events at Grubori with terrorist activities. We felt that this was an evident attempt to cover up the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did it come to your attention. Again I know you had access to UN reports, ICRC reports, various sources of information. Did you know about on the 18th of August, a meeting with the UN between the UN and General Cermak, an individual named Mr. Al-Alfi, recorded in that meeting there when General Cermak was informed about villages being looted and burnt. General Cermak making his comments about sharing his concern with the UN and expressing his unhappiness about its continuation. Something you knew about or not?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to know this later on, two weeks later, once Mr. Cicak had spoken to UN representatives. I didn't have direct contacts with them at that time. On their part, they only set us reports about victims and not about their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: On that basis were you privy to or not information, again, from the UN concerning a meeting they had with Mr. Cermak on the 24th of August, where the UN brought to Mr. Cermak's attention the continuation of burning houses and looting and asked him to stop such acts. He accepted this fact, as is recorded in this note of the meeting, regarding the continuation of such incidents and attributed to them to people entering the area wearing HV uniforms and to civilians taking revenge, stating that: "The area was very vast and that he would be lying if he told us that nothing of this sort would continue to happen but that he had informed us, the UN, that he had already issued orders to the civilian and military personnel to stop such acts." Were those intentions of Mr. Cermak something that came, again, to your radar?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat this, as a non-governmental organisation, we had contacts with international organisations to the extent that they knew what we were dealing and then would report to us on dead bodies that were found. They did not report to us on their political administrative or other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One last document. D59 on to the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I know that you reviewed and had access to media articles because many of them are cited within the report, Mr. Puhovski. I'd like you to take a look at this article before I conclude this section and ask you whether or not this ever came to your attention. It's a piece concerning General Cermak, talking about there being no place for looters in the HV. If you could read that and let me know whether or not you ever saw that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this, and there was an extended version of this, which was published one or two days later in the Vjesnik daily. So I'm familiar with both.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have approximately another 15 to 20 minutes questioning to complete, which I hope will keep me relatively in line with my estimate. I wonder if Your Honour would care to take the break now and for me to resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the break now. And then for the second in line, there will not be much time left today for cross-examination. We take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, we received an e-mail by the Cermak Defence on videolink. It's Friday, and if a videolink has to be organised, the registry would like to start as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The General Gotovina Defence has no objection to the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As well we are not opposing the videolink, but we are opposing the protective measures. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another matter. The urgency is in the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So no problem with the videolink as it refers to Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have reviewed the questions that I had, and in fact I have covered everything that I wanted to cover with Mr. Puhovski, and I thank him for answering my questions. Can I just answer one of Your Honours' questions which related to whether or not a comprehensive analysis had been done in respect of the tables or whether they were examples only. I have had confirmation from my team that was a comprehensive analysis, and those were the elements that were drawn out in the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for that information. I think you also owed me a review or whether it was 27 -- no, 17, 28 -- for the last two they know that they are included in a list which would be maximum 28 and minimum 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I do owe you that review, and I would like to be able to pass that information to the Chamber later today, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just in order to have things clearly on the record, the relatively large portion you read from a statement which is MFIed is -- I would like to emphasize that that is not in evidence, and although I'm not perfectly clear about how the link with the questions was, I'd like to -- to put that clearly on the record. Then next in line will be you Mr. Misetic. Thank you Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. And you're invited to conclude in 25 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to start off by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could turn to the HHO report at page 153 in the English in e-court and 146 in the B/C/S. This is 65 ter 4674.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I'm putting up on the screen, Professor. This is the portion of the report that deals with alleged civilian killings in Knin, and you will see that there is one reference to one individual being killed by a grenade in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can pull that up. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is entry number 212 for an individual named Momcilo Marjanovic. Do you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now my question is, as it relates to Knin, the only individual identified by the HHO to have been killed by shelling or a grenade in Knin that was a civilian is in fact Momcilo Marjanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In terms of the HHO's work, did family members of people come forward to you with the names of any individuals, loved ones, friends, et cetera, whom they said had been killed in the shelling of Knin, other than someone who gave you information about Mr. Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat, we received several hundreds of reports of people claiming that their family members disappeared in various locations from Knin to Hrvatska Kostajnica. We checked many of those allegations, although some we were unable to check. Some were proven false, whereas others were not. That's all can I tell you about in Knin in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Marjanovic specifically, did you ever obtain any information that in fact he was a high-ranking official of the Knin SUP or the Secretariat of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I learned that from an article, from the Belgrade Politika, I believe, a Belgrade paper. In that context he was referred to as such in 1997 or 1998. However, his title seemed irrelevant to us in relation to the fact that he was killed by a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to a different topic, do you have any familiarity with an incident that occurred I believe up in Sector North with Serbian RSK tanks running over their own civilians in a column. Are you familiar with such an incident?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received that by way of a report from the Helsinki Committee of Republika Srpska sometime in spring 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Since you have some knowledge, let me show you a video-clip of what allegedly took place and then I will ask you a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, this clip is 1D67-0218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, although Ms. Frolich does not object, of course, as soon as we move to Sector North, I usually hear many voices saying that that is irrelevant for our case, or is that only for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a reason, and that is -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have considered it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... carefully so that we do not -- I mean, if behaviour of one party in Sector North is relevant, it may be for the other as well. But if there is any specific matter then we'll wait and see, and it's now on the record that you have carefully considered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will tell you essentially what my question will be, is with respect it the -- the report talks about missing people. Obviously, some people started off in Sector South and wound up in the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. that's sufficient explanation for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] Here we see this was one of the SDS officials in the area of Komogovina. We possess his other documents as well. This is a column of Serb refugees they let out of Petrinja to travel via Popovaca 1.03.12 towards Lipovjani. This is the entrance into the memorial area Samarica which was an extremely difficult terrain to pass through, as it is a mountainous and woody area, which the Serbs side had quite successfully fortified with ample ammunition and many shelters. Almost every Serb village had an ammunition warehouse next to it. This is it an important piece of information. Yes, this is a horrific site we have never before seen. Five kilometres of horror and tragedy, where the Serb Chetnik army of Mile Novakovic fled from the sudden courageous incursion of the Croatian army, and in a panic, flight of tanks ran over its own column of refugees as they were preventing their cross over to the Bosnian side. In this way they were able to save part of their heavy weaponry, but they killed many. Precisely. In the panicked fear they wanted to flee as soon as possible, forgetting about their other population, their civilians who fleeing as well, clogged the road, a few kilometres before Dvor Na Uni, and simply when the Croatian army in its second incursion caught up with them, they simply ran their tanks over the civilians. Do we know how people were killed there? Well, hundreds of people died there, and believe me, I would have been better off had I never seen such horror. This is the moment they reached the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes, we will hear about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Puhovski, do you have, first of all, any information about the number of people that may have been run over there in that column of refugees?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything with any degree of certainty. I seem to recall the figure of 82 from the report of the RS Helsinki Committee. However, I saw that report a number of years ago, and I don't know whether it is correct. What I am certain though that it was 100. I couldn't verify it any further. I can only refer you to the report we received from their Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the civilians that were up in that area had been civilians who started off in Sector South and would have been travelling up through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that much. I only know that five or six people from the area of Hrvatska Kostajnica were confirmed as being in that column. That's what I can tell you. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any other incidents in addition to this one where Serbian forces in their effort to escape may have caused injury or death to any refugees in their own columns?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our report, there is a mention of a Serb plane opening fire and hitting several civilians. They claimed it was a Croatian plane. But from various testimonies, one could clearly conclude it was a Serb plane. I cannot recall off the cuff what page of the report that was. We also had reports of three or four our situations in which the smaller columns which were supposed to join the main one were stopped by units of the so-called RSK in withdrawal, and there were arguments, sometimes violent, as refers the part just following Petrinja, we had information of a skirmish where three or four people were killed. However we had only one source of that and, as such, we did not enter it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puhovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D67-0218 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Frolich, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: This heading HTV Slikom na sliku is this from the original programming, or is that what was superimposed by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We put the title of the programme and the date of the programme on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Yes. Other than, obviously, the geographical relevance, we do not have any objections to the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for me to understand completely what exactly -- and I made similar comments this morning to -- in relation to Prosecution Exhibit. What exactly does it add? And what exactly is the relevance apart from that people who had apparently left Sector South encountered a rather misfortune, perhaps at least some of them in Sector North? The pictures are such. I'm just wondering whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The report has an entire section on missing people, and to the accident that that is one explanation for why people could be missing, I think it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say without the images, the story would be exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, without the images, then they could be more disputed in closing argument than with the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, yes. Okay. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video-clip and the transcript will become exhibit number D1308.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, I'd like to ask you about some comments you made to a documentary producer. Do you recall being interviewed by a producer about Jack Baric about a documentary being made about General Gotovina in October 2006?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to play a clip of that interview. This is from the documentary film, Gotovina -- the interview took place on the 11th of October, 2006. Madam Registrar, it is 1D67-0248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second please. One second. It's not transcribed. I heard French translation. And then, of course, on the basis of that French translation, there will be a French transcript being made, although not in this country. Could we re-start -- have you received the transcript? Have the transcript been distributed? Because we all know that if there's a live recording, that no one is able to follow that at the right speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm advised there is a transcript that has been sent, and I should ask the English booth to read from the transcript, so that I guess things are slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a new procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: Just give me a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a spare copy, then the transcript could be produced in the usual way. I think, Madam Registrar, is already assisting. So let re-start the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "In my understanding, the analysis that was prepared by the Helsinki Committee, most of the killings were basically results of attempts to plunder the houses, to take everything that was found in the houses. And, in average, it would look like this. Half past 11.00 in the night, there was no electricity for 30 kilometres after the war in a small village 15 kilometres from Knin in the mountains, a group of three or four Croat citizens, some of them in uniform, some of them without uniforms, having one week from one of the towns in Dalmatia or in Lika, would try to enter a Serbian house to take everything that was there, and found out that suddenly the house was not empty. The first four houses in the village were empty because most of the people have left the area. And in the fifth house, they would find an old couple of, let's say, 65, 70, 75 years, and they would kill them after awaking them with their entrance because they didn't want to have witnesses. That's one part. Another part was during the operation when they were killing some of these civilians for revenge. But also because they were somehow expecting them to fight and not to just to evacuate the area. There is a very simple fact that practically no one is ready to say publicly the whole operation was realized, it was completed, in the pace of 145 square kilometres per hour. This is more like a safari than the military operation, and this is a mountain area. So if you have such a pace, you all the time watch behind your back because you believe they may be trying to entrap you, and they were somewhere behind in" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think all the translations have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, you seem to be describing there some of the factors that were involved in how people were killed. Do you wish to add anything to what we saw you say on the film there?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing has changed since. This is a post-factum analysis pursuant to the information we had following our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now at one point in the video you say that on average what would happen is three or four people would come into a village essentially looking to steal and would happen upon people unexpectedly and would kill them. When you say "on average," was that a typical situation in terms of what happened with many of the people killed after Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a hypothetical situation. It was supposed to illustrate -- perhaps I should have said it would have been a typical situation for what we were able to ascertain in several dozens of cases. People were found in their bedrooms or on the stairs from the first floor to the ground floor coming down, and there would only be one couple left behind in a hamlet. That brought us to the conclusions that I used in this hypothetical situation, which basically corresponded to a number of very real situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President I tender 1D67-0248 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Professor Puhovski, in your supplemental statement at paragraph 23, which is P2317, you comment that no one ever mentioned General Ante Gotovina in relation to the crimes. And I was wondering if you could further expound on that. When you say "no one," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, and when I say we, I have in mind our colleague who worked in the field, tried to put as many open questions as possible without any suggestions in terms of content. Based on such questions, the answers varied. For example, one of them was were there any military units in close proximity to a location where a body was found, and then we would get answers Croats, Serbs, this unit, or that unit. And then people would frequently volunteer information without being asked specifically. They would provide us with names of people whom they believed were responsible, whether they were commanders or some such. In one of my answers to the Prosecution, I said that Mr. Gotovina's name was never mentioned in any of such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could take you back for a moment, Professor, 65 ter 7150, which - let me see - that is Exhibit P2320, Madam Registrar. Now, Professor, this is the article that you drafted, I believe you said in August 1995, although it's misdated as May 1995. And you talk about -- in the second paragraph it says: "The military action was also a brilliantly organised example of ethnic cleansing. The speed of the Croatian victory came as a surprise for many diplomates and analysts." And then it says: "But the Serbs in Krajina, at least among the leadership, we were not surprised at all. From the very beginning of the action, they were not -- they were ready not only to flee but even to organise the escape of the entire population of their self-declared state. Indeed, Knin propaganda over the years - that Serbs could never safely live within Croatia - ultimately contributed to their flight." Before I move to the next part of your essay, I wanted to stop there and ask if could you further expand on what you know about the organisation of the escape of the entire population.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know three things: First, one week before the operation began, when there were negotiations about the Z-4 plan in the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, they began organizing the so-called points that were supposed to use to extract the population. I know that from conversations with several people who were in the civilian and military apparatus of that entity whom I met after the war. I also saw some documents to that effect. At that time, however, I knew only two things. One, that the strongest units had been withdrawn from Republika Srpska Krajina. I can perhaps illustrate that by way of an anecdote. On the second day of Operation Storm, I came to the main square in Zagreb Bana Jelacica Square and one -- I was one of the five people at the square. It was completely empty. Partly it was because it was the summer season, but partly because many expected that there would be even heavier bombardment of Zagreb than the one that had occurred in May after Operation Flash. Everyone presumed this is was a bigger operation with bigger consequences. No one knew that the rocket systems had been withdrawn, taken out of the hands of those in Knin. It turned out that they were unable to organise themselves and that their army was unable to defend. All of the people, or at least a very high percentage of the people from the area, had planned routes to leave their homes and that became evident in the course of the first few days. This text was drafted on the 18th or the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before you continue, we will need the time, and in order to avoid clashes with other Trial Chambers, I would invite you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I assure you, Judge, I will be disciplined and stop on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a word some people use, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have one question left on this document, and we can stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in the upper left-hand corner, you talk about the Croatian army facilitated the population movement, and you say that this was done -- it says the details including the targeting of Knin and other cities and treatment of civilians during mop-up actions remain to be fully investigated. But, you say: "At the same time, in every Croatian manoeuvre, openings were provided. The Croatian army declined completely to surround any Serbian town, escape routes marked and controlled by both Croatian forces and the UN were not only used by civilians but also by complete units of the Serbian Krajina forces ..." My question to you was, when you were writing this, did you think there might be a military logic in actually allowing military and civilians to leave, rather than encircling them and potentially causing greater bloodshed in a -- in a siege-type situation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PUHOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made several public statements on that. And I said that if there exists an indirect or direct agreement between Belgrade and Zagreb, then I supported it. I was quite clear on that. My personal view is, and, of course, I'm not a military expert, that the intention was -- my personal view is that the intention was to actually allow the military units to smoothly leave the area, although I was not an expert enough to know if this was realistically possible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions today. We'll pick up on Monday, but we have to deal with other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, I'd like to instruct you as I did before that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony already given or still to be given, and we would like to see you back. Unfortunately, we have to take another 20 minutes to deal with other matters, but we'd like to see you back on Monday, the 16th of February, 9.00 in the morning. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put a question to Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I count on me leaving The Hague on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Tuesday should be no problem. But I don't know what time you had in mind. Would you mean to finish on Monday and then to leave on Tuesday or to -- because if I look at our --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I was told yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your presence, I'll ask Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will certainly finish on Monday. But as you recall, I think you recall we have another witness on Monday as well, so I don't know how we're going to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... And I think you said you would need two sessions or a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I say two sessions. I'm well on my way, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we try to do our utmost best. I don't know what we are on Tuesday scheduled for, morning or afternoon. Your travel arrangement, Mr. Puhovski, are to leave at what time on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was to leave on the only direct flight there is, it's 11.00 a.m., if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll further -- first of all, I'll speak with the parties and see -- and we'll also see whether we can get any additional time on Monday, in case we might not be able to finish. Mr. Mikulicic, could you give already on the basis of what you have heard until now, a further estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will stay with my previous estimation, that means two sessions, but I will try to squeeze it up as more as I could able to do it because that depends also on Mr. Misetic cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. FROLICH
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point I have only a few points to raise with the witness on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would not need more time. Madam Registrar, could we inquire into what our possibilities would be for Monday in the afternoon, because Monday morning might be just not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All courtrooms are booked for Monday in the afternoon. The only other way out, I was just looking at today's court schedule, I don't know whether there would be, of course, it is very late for the registry, I am aware of that. But to organise it all, but just the parties would, they oppose against --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be agreeable to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: No opposition, but if there was a different courtroom, then that would be great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I noted it's extremely late, but at least there is no other Chamber using this courtroom or any of the other two courtrooms this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that could be of any assistance, I'm familiar with the flight schedule for Zagreb, and there is also a flight via Frankfurt on 5.00 in the afternoon, so maybe it could be of if any help for our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Puhovski, you see that all of us are trying to accommodate you as good as possible, so to take care that you Tuesday evening at home again. Whatever course it will take is uncertain at this moment. I've given you my instructions, we would like to see you back, most likely on Monday, unless you are here within one hour from now, then we would like to continue this afternoon, but if not within one hour, then please feel free to spend your time as you deem fit. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Puhovski out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give an opportunity to the parties to make submissions, in total, ten minutes for each. I'd like to read a statement from the Chamber. The Chamber gives a short statement with regard to tendering evidence at this late stage of the proceedings. As the Chamber set out in its Scheduling Order of the 6th of February of this year, the Prosecution's case is expected to end no later than the week of the 2nd of March, 2009. This is just a few weeks away. Although the Prosecution, in principle, is allowed to introduce evidence until its last day of its case, it must do so in a responsible way. This includes giving the Defence and the Chamber proper time to consider its submissions and the documentation it seeks to tender. The Chamber reminds the Prosecution that it prefers, to the extent possible, to have evidence introduced in a meaningful way in court with proper contextualisation and explanation by witness who is are in a position to do so. When it comes to bar table submissions, the Chamber has given guidance about how these should be presented to best assist the other party and the Chamber. However, the Chamber also emphasizes that the Prosecution must carefully select those documents or passages that are important and relevant enough to merit being tendered into evidence and only make such documents or passages part of their bar table submissions. On the 11th of February, 2009, the Prosecution filed its motion for admission into evidence of the statements of Ivan Cermak and Mladen Markac. Although we have not yet received the response to that motion, I -- the Chamber wants already to make some observations in this respect. These statements are, all together, almost 1200 pages long. It is it unclear to the Chamber why the Prosecution waited until the very end of its case to submit this seemingly important motion, giving the Defence and the Chamber very limited time to consider it. Moreover, tendering evidence in this way appears to shift the task of the Prosecution to identify relevant and probative material that it believes supports its case, onto the Chamber. In this respect, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution, in the motion, only refers to about 300 out of the 1200 pages as containing evidence that is relevant and probative of issues to the case. Therefore, the Chamber urges the Prosecution to carefully review the statements of Ivan Cermak and Mladen Markac and select those portions that it considers would most assist the Chamber in determining important issues in this case. And for the remaining weeks of the Prosecution's case, the Chamber urges the parties to act in such a way as to enable the Chamber to decide on the admission of all outstanding evidence by the last day of the Prosecution's case. This concludes the Chamber's statement, and as may have been clear from the statement, does not in any way anticipate on whatever decision would be taken on the motion because we haven't heard yet from the Defence. Then I promised both parties ten minutes for submissions. No other chamber will sit so even if we would go seven or eight minutes beyond or time, I'd like to give an opportunity, I think Prosecution first. Mr. Tieger, and I will strictly keep to you ten minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again, in view of the confidentiality, do we have to -- I asked the question about this this morning. Your submissions will be made in public, although some part of the submissions are confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I had anticipated, Your Honour, please, and don't take this against my time, that we would be in closed session in light of the earlier filings. I can try to deal with it on an argument-by-argument basis, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We will then turn into closed session, but I think I raised specifically this morning the confidentiality, and if you say matters stand as they are, then we move into private session, I would say would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was communicated to me in respect of one part of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the motion and confidential Annex C and the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could move into private session first, and then I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session, and let's then proceed not to loose further time. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But first wait for the confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until the 16th of February, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.
